questions.stem: What is the primary function of a switch in a network?

options.text: To broadcast frames to all ports
To forward frames to specific ports based on MAC addresses
To route packets based on IP addresses
To convert digital signals to analog signals

questions.explanation: Switches operate at the data link layer and use MAC addresses to forward frames to the appropriate port, unlike hubs which broadcast to all ports or routers which use IP addresses.

questions.stem: How does a switch learn which port reaches a specific MAC address?

options.text: By broadcasting frames to all ports
By examining the destination MAC address of incoming frames
By examining the source MAC address of incoming frames

questions.explanation: Switches learn MAC addresses by examining the source MAC address of incoming frames and updating their MAC address table to associate the address with the port on which the frame was received.

questions.stem: Which layer of the OSI model do switches operate on?
questions.explanation: Switches operate at the Data Link Layer (Layer 2) of the OSI model, where they forward frames based on MAC addresses. This is distinct from routers, which operate at the Network Layer (Layer 3).

questions.stem: What field in an Ethernet frame is used for error checking?
questions.explanation: The Frame Check Sequence (FCS) is used for error checking in Ethernet frames. It allows the receiving device to detect errors in the frame by comparing the calculated FCS with the received FCS.

questions.explanation: When the switch receives the frame, it will add an entry to its MAC address table associating the source MAC address 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E with Port 4. Since the table was initially empty, it will have one entry after processing the frame.

questions.stem: Explain the difference between a switch and a hub in terms of data forwarding.
markingGuide: Switches forward frames to specific ports based on MAC addresses.
Hubs broadcast frames to all ports regardless of the destination.
Switches reduce network congestion by directing frames only to the intended recipient.
Hubs can lead to network inefficiencies due to unnecessary data transmission.
questions.explanation: Switches and hubs differ significantly in how they handle data forwarding. Switches use MAC addresses to forward frames to the correct port, which minimizes unnecessary data traffic and reduces congestion. In contrast, hubs broadcast frames to all ports, which can lead to inefficiencies and increased network traffic.

questions.stem: Which of the following fields is NOT part of a standard Ethernet frame?
questions.explanation: A standard Ethernet frame includes fields such as Destination MAC Address, Source MAC Address, EtherType, Payload, and Frame Check Sequence (FCS). The IP Address is not part of the Ethernet frame itself; it is part of the data carried within the frame.

questions.stem: What happens if a switch receives a frame with a destination MAC address not in its MAC address table?

options.text: The switch broadcasts the frame to all ports except the incoming port
The switch forwards the frame to a random port
The switch sends the frame back to the sender

questions.explanation: If a switch receives a frame with a destination MAC address not in its MAC address table, it will broadcast the frame to all ports except the one it was received on. This ensures that the frame reaches its intended recipient if it is connected to the network.

questions.stem: Describe how a switch can prevent broadcast storms in a network.
markingGuide: Switches can implement VLANs to segment network traffic.
Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) can be used to prevent loops in the network.
Switches can limit the rate of broadcast traffic.
Proper network design and configuration can minimize the risk of broadcast storms.
questions.explanation: Switches can prevent broadcast storms by using techniques such as VLANs to segment traffic, implementing Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) to prevent loops, and limiting the rate of broadcast traffic. Proper network design and configuration are also critical in minimizing the risk of broadcast storms.
